notes.meaning: The writer begins with the only bright ray of comfort in the whole psalm by calling the Lord the God of his salvation. Even in deep sorrow, he still looks to God alone for help and pours out his heart day and night. His constant crying shows that pain drives him straight to prayer rather than away from the Lord.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine understood the entire psalm as the voice of Christ praying, taking "day" to mean seasons of peace and "night" to mean times of disaster.

notes.meaning: The psalmist asks God to welcome his prayer like a king welcoming an ambassador. He begs God to bend down and listen closely to his tearful cry. Because he has prayed without ceasing, he pleads that his words will not be cast aside.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine explained that God inclining his ear describes his tender compassion rather than a physical body, showing that he lovingly stoops to hear the humble.

notes.meaning: His inner life is completely flooded with grief, like a cup filled to the very brim. He feels that his strength is almost gone and that he is standing at the edge of the grave. The Hebrew word Sheol speaks of the mysterious place of the dead, and the writer feels ready to slip into it.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine connected this sorrow directly to Jesus in Gethsemane saying his soul was sorrowful unto death, showing that Christ took on human grief without taking on human sin.

notes.meaning: People around the psalmist have given up on him and treat him as good as dead. Any natural vigor he once possessed is completely gone, leaving him weak and helpless. He feels counted among those who are already descending into the pit of the grave.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine saw the pit as the deep misery of death, noting that those who killed Jesus thought he was just an ordinary man without power to save himself.

notes.meaning: He feels like a wounded soldier left behind among the corpses on a battlefield. It seems to him as though he is cut off from God's active protection and set aside from human life. He is describing how things feel in his dark depression, not what God is actually doing.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interpreted being set free among the dead as pointing to Christ, who alone among men was free from sin and laid down his life willingly.

notes.meaning: The writer sees God's sovereign hand behind the painful trial he is enduring. He compares his misery to being locked away in a dark, slimy pit with no beam of light. Acknowledging that God is in charge of his pain shows real faith, even when he cannot see a way out.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine understood the lowest pit as the very bottom of human sorrow and punishment.

notes.meaning: God's displeasure feels like a crushing weight pressing down on his chest. Hardships crash over him one after another, like giant ocean waves threatening to drown him. The word Selah provides a short pause, like a swimmer coming up for air before the next wave hits.

His suffering is made worse because his closest friends have abandoned him and stay far away. His condition may have been an illness like leprosy, which forced sick people into quarantine away from society. He feels locked up in a lonely prison of misery with no escape.

Constant weeping has exhausted his eyes and worn away his sight. Yet even while shedding bitter tears, he continues to call out to the Lord every single day. Stretching out his hands was the natural way God's people reached out to plead for his help.

The psalmist pleads for God to rescue him quickly before his life on earth ends. In Old Testament times, the realm of the dead was viewed as a shadowy place where people no longer participated in public worship. He asks how he can praise God for saving him if he is already dead and gone.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine applied the dead to people who are spiritually dead in heart, who refuse to turn to God in praise even when they witness Christ's miracles.

notes.meaning: The writer appeals to God's loyal love and his promise-keeping faithfulness. If God lets his servant die in despair, there will be no one left in that silent grave to speak of God's goodness. He wants to live so he can openly tell others how true God is to his word.

The grave is described as a land of darkness and forgetfulness, where memory fades and the dead are forgotten by the living. The psalmist asks how God's saving deeds and justice can be proclaimed in such an unseen place. He longs to witness and declare God's righteousness while still alive on earth.

Even though relief has not arrived, the psalmist firmly resolves to keep crying out to the Lord. He plans to wake up early in the morning so his prayer can greet God before the busy day begins. Delaying the answer tests his patience, but it will not stop him from praying.

The deepest pain for a servant of God is feeling that the Lord has turned away his face. The psalmist asks with humble boldness why he seems rejected, searching for the reason behind his trouble. He cannot bear to lose the comforting light of God's presence.

His sorrows are not new; he has lived with sickness, weakness, and fear ever since his youth. The constant dread of God's judgment has worn down his strength to the point of utter confusion and despair. Even after a lifetime of distress, he still turns his broken spirit toward God.

God's fierce displeasure feels like a fiery flood sweeping over his soul. Terrifying thoughts of divine judgment have beaten him down until he feels completely undone. Although the sufferer feels hopelessly cut off, God never actually abandons his true children.

Troubles surround him like rising floodwaters that creep into every crack and offer no way out. These trials press in from every side from morning until night, giving him no rest. He feels as though he is being swallowed alive by deep distress.

The psalm ends without any sudden word of joy, mourning that every friend and loved one has been taken away. With no human comfort left, thick darkness feels like the only companion remaining beside him. Yet by ending his song in direct conversation with the Lord, the writer shows that real faith still clings to God in the dark.
